edits.before: Secure aggregation ran four stages: setup, key sharing, masked-vector collection and unmasking. The server used SecAggPlusWorkflow and clients used secaggplus_mod, with identifiers setup, share_keys, collect_masked_vectors and unmask. Message checks verified expected fields and the absence of plaintext individual updates in aggregation replies. Each client created three shares of both its private-mask seed and the private key used to derive pairwise masks. Two shares were required to reconstruct either secret for unmasking. Nevertheless, every accepted stage required all three clients’ replies. Missing replies stopped the workflow, without fallback to ordinary FedAvg.
after: Secure aggregation proceeded through setup, key sharing, masked-vector collection and unmasking. Message checks verified expected fields and the absence of plaintext individual updates in aggregation replies. Every accepted stage required all three clients’ replies; missing replies stopped the workflow without fallback to ordinary FedAvg. Table 3.5 records the share and reconstruction settings, and Appendix B.5 gives the implementation identifiers.

edits.before: The security interpretation follows the assumptions in Section 2.4 and implementation boundary in Section 3.8. FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017) and secure aggregation (Bonawitz et al., 2017; Bell et al., 2020; Li et al., 2022) supply the established components. Bell et al.’s proofs and component benchmarks concern specified corruption, dropout and public-key conditions; Li et al. assume authenticated, encrypted links and exclude communication latency from simulation. The local workflows used different diagnostics and no TLS. Their elapsed-time difference measures those workflows; protocol analyses and local checks have distinct evidential roles.
after: FedAvg (McMahan et al., 2017) and secure aggregation (Bonawitz et al., 2017; Bell et al., 2020) supply the established components, under the assumptions and implementation boundary in Sections 2.4 and 3.8. Local checks in Section 4.11 address selected implementation behaviours.

edits.before: False alerts are the main obstacle to practical use. In the primary test, FedAvg with SecAgg+ had mean precision of approximately 46–50% and about 72–87 false alerts per 1,000 legitimate sessions across the two sampling conditions. The secondary test used a different legitimate denominator: only unusual legitimate activity, which all three methods frequently flagged (Table 4.7). These benchmark rates describe alert selectivity, not an estimated hospital review workload.

Neither explanations of individual alerts nor the usefulness of these review procedures was evaluated here. Both remain requirements for a future application study.

edits.before: The local tests support selected masking-helper, message-check and numerical-aggregation behaviours. These checks neither measured leakage nor established cryptographic certification, arbitrary-collusion resistance, host-administrator isolation or TLS protection (Section 4.11; Appendix C.7).
